title: Silent japa

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri: the oldest mantra, asking the sun to light up our minds. Your line was light, illuminate the mind. Today, the mantra goes quiet.

You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself. Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? The tradition noticed this long ago. Say a mantra out loud long enough, and one day you catch it going on inside you while you're doing something else entirely. Nobody's saying it. It's saying itself. There's a word for that.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?` → `NOBODY IS SAYING IT.`

segments.voice: Japa comes three ways. Out loud, as you did with Hare Krishna, is vachika, spoken. Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. Silent, only in the mind, is manasika, mental. Several old texts and teachers rank these, and they put the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, they say, the deeper it goes in. Not because out loud is wrong, but because silent japa has nowhere to hide. No sound to lean on, just you and the mantra. Then there's a fourth thing, which isn't really a way of doing japa at all: ajapa. The a at the front means not. Not-repeating: the mantra that happens without anyone doing it. The yoga traditions describe it with the breath. Some teachers say the in-breath makes a soft sound like so, and the out-breath a sound like ham. So-ham, a Sanskrit phrase meaning I am that. The old texts say every living being repeats it with every breath, all day and all night, thousands of times a day, without knowing. They call it the ajapa gayatri, the Gayatri that isn't said. You can't force ajapa; you can only notice it. So you start with silent japa, then gradually let go of saying it, and see if the breath carries it on. It says itself.
screen: `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, SILENT.` · `THE QUIETER, THE DEEPER.` · `AJAPA — NOT-REPEATING.` · `SO ON THE IN-BREATH, HAM ON THE OUT.` · then, large: `IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle into your breath and say your mantra silently, the one that fits or simply so-ham: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out, no lips, no whisper. After a while, stop saying it on purpose and just listen for the so and the ham in the breath. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently, and let go again.
Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.
Your line: it says itself. The breath has been saying it all along. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

notes: Ajapa gayatri / hamsa and the count of 21,600 breaths per day: in the Dhyanabindu Upanishad and hatha/tantra texts; the script says 'thousands of times a day' and puts 21,600 only in the trapdoor. Confirm citation.
Which sound goes with which breath: some teach so on the in-breath and ham on the out (so-ham); others the reverse (ham-sa). Script says 'some teachers say'. Confirm.
Ranking of the three kinds of japa: Manusmriti 2.85 ranks muttered (upamshu) above ritual and mental higher still; later texts rank vachika < upamshu < manasika. Confirm.
